name: Minoxidil sulfate

card.summary: The active form of minoxidil, produced in the scalp by sulfotransferase enzymes, through which minoxidil is understood to help regrow hair.
card.note: Minoxidil itself is the product sold; response is linked to scalp enzyme levels.

quick.overview:
Minoxidil sulfate is the active metabolite of minoxidil, the hair-loss treatment sold as Rogaine and Regaine. Minoxidil is a prodrug, meaning scalp enzymes convert it to the sulfate form.

Hair regrowth from minoxidil can improve hair density and coverage in pattern hair loss, usually appearing after 2 to 4 months with maximum effect around 12 months. Research has asked whether boosting the conversion enzyme improves response.
quick.how: People use minoxidil, not the sulfate itself; the conversion happens in the follicle. Some studies have looked at adding tretinoin or an enzyme-boosting product to raise response.
quick.risks: Minoxidil effects are reversible and stopping leads to loss again. Aspirin and salicylic acid may inhibit sulfotransferase activity according to Wikipedia. See the minoxidil entry for side effects.

lead: Minoxidil sulfate is the active form of minoxidil. Minoxidil itself is a prodrug, converted by sulfotransferase enzymes into the sulfate, which forms both systemically and inside hair follicles.[1][2] In hair follicles SULT1A1 is the main enzyme.[1]

Because the sulfate form is responsible for the hair-growth effect, researchers have asked whether individual enzyme levels explain why some people respond better than others, and whether other products raise it. A randomised trial examined an enzyme booster applied before 5% minoxidil, and a study examined tretinoin as a way to upregulate follicular sulfotransferase in androgenetic alopecia patients.[3][4]
Minoxidil is understood to act partly as an ATP-sensitive potassium channel opener. A 1993 review noted that other potassium channel openers also maintain hair growth in cultured follicles.[5]

chain: Scalp sulfotransferase converts it to minoxidil sulfate
Follicles shift toward growth, giving denser hair
angle.text: Minoxidil sulfate is the form believed to act on follicles; people use minoxidil to thicken thinning hair, and response is linked to SULT1A1 activity.[1][3]

paras: Several human cytosolic sulfotransferases can sulfate minoxidil; studies of scalp skin and platelets found multiple enzyme activities involved.[6][1] SULT1A1 expression has been linked to topical response.[1] Mechanism is not fully understood; proposed contributors include potassium channel opening and growth factors such as VEGF.[1]

The sulfate was reported to be about 14 times more potent than minoxidil in stimulating cysteine incorporation in cultured rodent follicles.[1] Aspirin and salicylic acid can inhibit sulfotransferase activity, and paracetamol may interfere with sulfate formation.[1]

Upjohn developed minoxidil in 1963, it was approved as an oral blood-pressure drug in 1979, and topical use for male baldness was approved by the FDA in 1988 as Rogaine, going over the counter in 1996.[1]

A randomised controlled trial in men tested a SULT1A1 enzyme booster applied before daily 5% minoxidil, motivated by the relatively low response rate to topical minoxidil.[3] A 2019 study reported that tretinoin enhanced minoxidil response in androgenetic alopecia patients by upregulating follicular sulfotransferase.[4] A 2026 paper examined minoxidil sulfate's effects on JAK/STAT signalling in alopecia areata.[7]

timeline.event: Topical minoxidil available over the counter.[1]
